To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

immobilization of the lower limbs for 2 week followed by rehabilitation does not change the expression of proteins or genes associated with muscle mass regulation, and that GAPDH, HAMDA, and S26 are not useful for normalization of RNA expression data.
immobilization and rehabilitation did not affect the phosphorylation or expression of Akt, mTor and their downstream targets.
immobilization does not induce expected changes in muscle mass signaling and that the use of GAPDH, HAMDA and S26 for normalization of RNA expression data should be questioned.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular regulation of muscle mass during immobilization and rehabilitation, but the results are inconclusive.
the signaling of the Akt axis in human muscle and its relation to immobilization-induced atrophy.
the molecular regulation in rehabilitation of immobilization-atrophied muscle.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the changes in protein mass with immobilization and subsequent normalization were not accompanied by changes in protein expression and phosphorylations of the measured proteins along the Akt axis.

we did not find any evidence of the expected changes in the expression or phosphorylation of the investigated proteins in response to immobilization and rehabilitation, and that the use of these proteins for normalization of mRNA data in immobilization studies is not recommended.
the molecular signaling pathways involved in the loss of muscle mass associated with lower limb immobilization are still poorly understood and require more studies to elucidate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the changes in muscle protein mass associated with immobilized muscle are not accompanied by changes in protein synthesis and degradation signaling or mRNA levels of key muscle mass regulators.
immobilization and rehabilitation do not affect the expression of the investigated proteins and mRNA, but that immobilization does affect the expression of putative housekeeping gene expression.
the molecular regulation of muscle atrophy and rehabilitation is complex and that further studies are required to elucidate the molecular regulation of these processes.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the regulation of muscle atrophy and hypertrophy is a complex and multi-faceted phenomenon, and that the use of only a few genes for normalization is not sufficient for the study of the regulation of muscle mass.
we have not been able to identify key molecular regulators in the muscle mass signaling with rehabilitation of immobilization induced muscle atrophy.
we did not observe any changes in the signaling pathways of muscle protein turnover with immobilization and subsequent rehabilitative interventions.
